lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 7 you studied adverts. Can you name two tricks they use? (A famous person, the bandwagon, a free gift, a health claim, small print.) Today: using honest persuasion to help people's health.
A health campaign helps people make a healthy choice: drink more water, sleep more, walk to school, be kind online. Speaking up for other people's health is called advocacy.
Plan it in steps. Survey to find the problem, and set a SMART aim. Choose your audience and one clear message. Run the campaign, then survey again and compare.
Start with evidence. In a survey, 45 of 150 pupils drank water at lunch: 45 ÷ 150 = 0.3, so 30%. A SMART aim: '50% of pupils drinking water at lunch by July.'
A good message is short, positive, true and says what to do. 'Refill at the fountain: water helps you focus.' Use facts with sources. Never shame anyone, or scare them with things that aren't true.
Know your audience. Younger pupils like games and pictures; older pupils like facts and choices; parents like clear reasons. Choose posters, an assembly, a short video or a stall.
Measure the change: ask the same question to the same group, before and after. Before 30%, after 50%: a rise of 50 − 30 = 20 percentage points. Then say what worked and what to change.
Try it in the world: run a mini campaign in your village or class, with a survey before and after. In LIFE, Talk & Deal practises pitching an idea clearly. Next: digital balance.

exercises.prompt: Advocacy means speaking up for other people's health.
exercises.hint: Think of the lesson's word for speaking up.
exercises.explain: True: a health campaign is advocacy, speaking up to help others choose healthily.

exercises.prompt: 45 of 150 pupils drank water at lunch. What percentage is that?
exercises.hint: Divide the part by the whole, then times 100.

choices: 50% of pupils drink water at lunch by July
exercises.hint: Look for a number and a date.
exercises.explain: It says what, how much and by when, so you can check whether it worked.

exercises.prompt: Put the campaign's steps in order.
exercises.hint: Evidence first, then an aim, then the message.
exercises.explain: Survey, aim, audience and message, run it, then survey again to see the change.

exercises.prompt: In the survey chart, which drink was most popular at lunch?
exercises.explain: The fizzy bar is tallest, at 60 of 150 pupils: the campaign's starting point.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best campaign message?
choices: Refill at the fountain: water helps you focus
Fizzy drinks will ruin your life
exercises.hint: A good message is positive, true and says what to do.
exercises.explain: It is short, true, kind and gives a clear action, with no shaming or scaring.

exercises.prompt: Before the campaign, 30% drank water at lunch; after it, 50%. By how many percentage points did it rise?
exercises.hint: Subtract the before from the after.

exercises.prompt: Match each audience to a good way to reach it.
exercises.hint: Think about what each group pays attention to.
exercises.explain: Young pupils: a game. Older pupils: facts. Parents: clear reasons. Everyone: an assembly.

exercises.prompt: Scaring people with things that aren't true is a good way to run a health campaign.
exercises.hint: Would you trust a campaign that lied to you?
exercises.explain: False: honest facts and positive messages work and keep trust; scare stories and shaming do not.

exercises.hint: Would it still be fair if everyone knew how it worked?
exercises.explain: Honest: sourced facts, a clear action, real results. Tricks: made-up claims and shaming.

exercises.prompt: A survey asked 200 pupils; 50 walked to school. What percentage walked?
Before the campaign, 20% of 150 pupils had breakfast; after it, 60%. How many more pupils is that?
exercises.hint: Find the rise in percentage points, then take that percentage of 150.

exercises.prompt: Why must the 'after' survey ask the same question to the same group?
choices: so the change is fair to compare
exercises.explain: Keeping the question and group the same means any change is down to the campaign.

items: plan what to change next time
exercises.explain: Survey the same way, compare, say what worked, and plan the next improvement.

exercises.prompt: The 'after' survey shows no change. What is the best next step?
choices: find out why and change the message
exercises.hint: An honest result is still useful information.
exercises.explain: Asking people why, then changing the message or the way it is shared, is how campaigns improve.
